prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B047 to B006 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. In round 1 I kept B006 as my first alternative for one stated reason, attribution: colleagues were proposing different trios and I said I would not put it first unless we could agree on a defensible split. That condition has now been met. All six members who prefer B006 name the same three people, and they arrive there by an argument I can follow: Kane and Mele wrote the Z2 and quantum spin Hall papers jointly, and Molenkamp's HgTe transport experiment is the first decisive observation of the predicted protected edge channels. The principle of theory plus first realisation is the one I would apply to any candidate, and it gives a compact citation here. On the science, the Z2 invariant is a new classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, the interpretation has been stable for almost two decades under transport, photoemission and scanning-probe tests, and the idea has reached well beyond one subfield. That breadth of consequence is where I judge B006 ahead of B047, which is concentrated in metrology even though its physics is excellent. I also say plainly that my opening ranking of B047 first was helped by field proximity, and that a first place from an atomic theorist for an atomic-physics candidate should be discounted.
statement.case_against: The attribution cost has not gone away, it has only been agreed on. The HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not credited and Zhang is deceased, and Hasan's first three-dimensional photoemission work and the Fu-Moore-Balents-Roy theory are left out. The citation should be worded narrowly around the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant so that it does not appear to recognise the 3D materials discovery. The 2016 prize for topological phases is a real overlap that must be answered in the text, and I find the answer convincing but not obviously decisive: the earlier prize rewarded topological transitions and Chern-type invariants without time-reversal symmetry, while Z2 insulators depend on spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry, a different class with different edge physics. Finally, B047 loses nothing scientifically by my move. Magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a separate invention from the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion control, with a quantified 1e-18 result, and I think a committee that awarded it would be on firm ground.

responses.point: Eriksson wrote that I worry the 2016 prize leaves less appetite for a second topological award, and responded that the Z2 insulators are a separate discovery of more consequence for materials.
responses.response: Two of you have attributed the 2016 worry to me, and so has the chair's summary, so I will correct it: my round-1 hesitation about B006 was attribution, not the 2016 overlap. On the overlap itself I now agree with you. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz honoured topological transitions and quantum Hall type invariants, whereas the Z2 insulator is protected by time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling and has its own experimental signature in the HgTe edge conductance. As an answer to the chair's question, I regard that as settled for me, provided the citation states the distinction. I also take your point that your own move from B017 to B006 rested on maturity, and I share the view that twisted bilayer graphene is a strong case in a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and says that omitting Hasan is the main weakness but that naming a single 3D experimental name is contestable.
responses.response: Your reasoning resolves the question I raised in round 1. The 3D observations involve competing materials (Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3) and a theory credit shared by Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore and Balents, so one extra experimental name would be hard to defend, while dropping Mele would split a joint paper. I answer the chair's second question directly: I do not hold that Hasan should replace Mele or Molenkamp. I also keep your point that the committee should not hide the cost; I would rather that the citation say openly that it is about the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant. I read your stated willingness to support the Hasan version as a fallback and would not oppose it, but I do not prefer it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first and argues that magic-wavelength trapping is a new principle, that the committee should not wait for the redefinition of the second, and that two atomic physicists should be challenged from outside.
responses.response: I still agree with you on the physics and the two names, and my agreement on not waiting for the redefinition of the second is complete: the discovery does not depend on a metrology-body decision. I am moving away from B047 as my preferred prize for different reasons than the ones you reject. Both of us have argued distinctness from 2005 and 2012, and no non-atomic member has said the argument fails, but several say they cannot test it. That is the external challenge you asked for, and I should not use it as a reason to hold the first place against a candidate whose attribution is now agreed and whose consequences reach more fields. I will keep B047 as my first alternative and would support it for a later year or as the committee's choice if the majority wishes. I also accept your suggestion that I disclose my atomic-physics proximity more fully, which I do below.

responses.point: Pearce adopts theory plus first realisation as the selection principle, would not wait for the redefinition of the second, and keeps B047 as first alternative because breadth across condensed matter favours B006.
responses.response: We now share the same principle and the same ordering, though I arrive here from the opposite side. Your remark that the committee should judge the discovery, not the subject label, is the answer to my own earlier worry about 2D versus 3D: the citation can honestly describe the 2D discovery and still stand as a topological insulator prize. As a reply to the chair's last question, I do not support B017 in 2026, and I do not support a two-part prize pairing B006 with B047, because Kane, Mele and Molenkamp plus Katori and Ye is five people and would force one of the pairs to be cut.

responses.point: Johansson, who ranks circuit QED first and has disclosed a conflict on B038, now prefers B006, and says a second superconducting-circuit award right after 2025 would be hard to justify.
responses.response: I agree with your decision to discount your own enthusiasm for B038 and with your timing argument. I keep B038 as my second alternative rather than rejecting it, because the transfer of cavity QED to circuits is a clean and mature idea. But Girvin's omission from the credited theory share, together with a second prize to the same community one year after 2025, leaves it behind B006 and B047 for me in 2026. Your point that B047 could be a second part is correct in principle, and I explain above why the three-person ceiling rules it out.

uncertainties: Whether the citation for B006 can be worded narrowly enough on the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant that it does not implicitly claim the 3D materials discovery or ignore the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.

Whether my move from B047 to B006 reflects a better judgement or only the removal of one concern (attribution); I cannot rule out that the shared atomic background of Kroll and myself led me to overrate B047 before and could lead me to underrate it now.
Whether ion-clock groups or other early lattice-clock proposers should share credit under B047, which the supplied names do not address; this affects only my alternative.
How much weight the committee should give to the 2016 overlap; I regard it as answerable but it is a judgement and not a measurement.
statement.conflict_note: No credited name on B006, B047 or B038 appears among my documented collaborators. I disclose field proximity to the atomic-physics entries (B047, B031, B034) and note that I have mentioned my own first-place support for B047 may have been influenced by it. Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato are not credited on any shortlisted part. I also note that Ursula Keller's group, with which I have collaborated, is at ETH Zurich, the institution of Andreas Wallraff (B038, my second alternative); no collaboration with Wallraff is documented, but I flag the institutional proximity. I have no documented tie to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp.
